title: Your First Round
objective: Understand what a motion, a side and a speech are — and what a judge actually rewards.

steps.heading: The three moving parts
steps.body: Every round has a motion (the statement being argued), two sides (For and Against), and speeches delivered in a fixed order. You win by giving the judge clearer reasons than your opponent — not by talking more, faster, or louder.

steps.heading: What judges reward
steps.body: Judges score six things on Debates.ch: argumentation, rebuttal, evidence, strategy, delivery and persuasion. A short, structured speech that answers the opponent beats a long stream of unconnected points every time.

steps.prompt: You're assigned Against on a motion you personally agree with. What should you do?
choices: Argue the Against case as well as you can
Concede early because the motion is right
Argue For anyway — honesty first
Refuse the round
steps.explanation: Debating is a skill exercise: you argue the assigned side. Arguing positions you disagree with is precisely what builds the muscle of understanding both sides.

steps.prompt: Which speech most impresses a judge?
choices: Three developed arguments with a clear comparison to the other side
Seven quick points with no development
One long emotional story
A detailed attack on the opponent's speaking style
steps.explanation: Depth and comparison beat quantity. Judges reward developed mechanisms and explicit weighing, not point-counting — and never personal attacks.

title: Anatomy of an Argument
objective: Build arguments with the claim → mechanism → example → impact structure.

steps.heading: Claims are not arguments
steps.body: "Homework should be banned" is a claim. An argument adds a mechanism (WHY it leads to something), an example (WHERE we've seen it), and an impact (WHO is better off and by how much). Missing mechanisms are the most common weakness at every level.

steps.heading: The four-step chain
steps.body: Claim: primary-school homework should go. Mechanism: young children learn through play and rest; homework displaces both and adds family conflict. Example: several school systems dropped it with no measured achievement loss. Impact: less stress for millions of families at no academic cost.

steps.prompt: "Social media is bad for teenagers, everyone knows that, so it should be restricted." What's missing?
choices: The mechanism — why and how it causes harm
A louder delivery
A longer conclusion
Nothing — it's complete
steps.explanation: "Everyone knows" is an appeal to popularity, not a mechanism. You need the causal chain: what specifically about the platforms produces what specific harm, for whom.

steps.prompt: Which sentence states an impact?
choices: As a result, a million commuters gain an hour a day with their families
Traffic congestion is caused by too many cars
Amsterdam built bicycle lanes in the 1970s
We propose congestion charging in city centres
steps.explanation: Impacts name who benefits and by how much. The others are a mechanism, an example and a proposal — all useful, but the impact is what the judge weighs.

title: Rebuttal That Actually Lands
objective: Attack the load-bearing premise of an argument instead of its wording.

steps.heading: Find the load-bearing premise
steps.body: Every argument rests on one premise that, if removed, collapses the rest. Rebuttal means identifying that premise and showing it is false, unproven, or outweighed — not disputing side details or restating your own case louder.

steps.heading: The four rebuttal moves
steps.body: Deny (the mechanism doesn't work), Mitigate (it works less than claimed), Outweigh (true, but our impact is bigger), Turn (their point actually helps us). The strongest rebuttals name the move: "Even if that's true, here's why it doesn't decide the round."

steps.prompt: Opponent: "A four-day week works because trials showed stable productivity." What is the load-bearing premise?
choices: That trial firms are representative of the whole economy
That workers enjoy three-day weekends
That productivity can be measured
That trials existed
steps.explanation: The trials happened and were measured — attacking that goes nowhere. The case collapses only if self-selected trial firms (often offices) don't generalise to hospitals, factories and shops.

steps.prompt: Which response is a "turn"?
choices: Your ban on plastic bags actually increases emissions, because cotton totes need 100+ uses to break even
Plastic bags aren't that bad
You didn't cite a source for that
Let me return to my own arguments
steps.explanation: A turn shows the opponent's policy produces the very harm they campaign against — their point becomes your evidence.

title: Evidence That Counts
objective: Choose evidence for relevance and reliability, and represent uncertainty honestly.

steps.heading: Relevant beats impressive
steps.body: A modest statistic that measures exactly what you claim beats a dramatic one that measures something nearby. Ask: does this evidence support my mechanism, or just my mood? And never invent precision — "roughly a third" said honestly outscores "34.7%" said falsely.

steps.heading: The credibility ladder
steps.body: Systematic reviews and official statistics sit at the top; single studies and institutional reports in the middle; anecdotes and headlines at the bottom. Anecdotes aren't worthless — they make mechanisms vivid — but they can't carry a causal claim alone.

steps.prompt: You half-remember a study but not its details. In a rated debate you should:
choices: Present it as an illustrative example and flag your uncertainty
Invent plausible numbers to sound rigorous
Cite it confidently anyway
Say nothing and hope
steps.explanation: Honest uncertainty preserves credibility and still does argumentative work. Fabricated precision is the fastest way to lose a judge — and on this platform, bots are penalised for it too.

steps.prompt: Motion: ban energy drinks for under-16s. Which evidence is MOST relevant?
choices: A cohort study linking teen energy-drink consumption to sleep disruption
Global caffeine market revenue figures
A celebrity saying they feel jittery
The number of energy-drink flavours available
steps.explanation: It measures the claimed harm, in the claimed population, with a causal design. Market size and celebrity feelings measure something else entirely.

title: Weighing: Why Yours Matters More
objective: Compare impacts explicitly on magnitude, probability, timeframe and reversibility.

steps.heading: Lists don't win rounds
steps.body: When both sides have standing arguments, judges look for weighing: which impact is bigger (magnitude), more likely (probability), sooner (timeframe), and harder to undo (reversibility)? The side that does this comparison controls how the round is decided.

steps.heading: Collapse before you close
steps.body: Strong debaters spend their final speech on the two or three clashes that decide the round and openly drop the rest. Answering everything shallowly is how you lose a round you were winning.

steps.prompt: Your impact: slow economic gains for millions. Theirs: rare but irreversible harms to a few. Your strongest weighing lever?
choices: Magnitude and probability — near-certain gains for millions outweigh rare edge cases
Repeat your mechanism louder
Concede — irreversibility always wins
Argue their harm doesn't matter at all
steps.explanation: Neither dimension auto-wins; you must argue the comparison. Claiming their harm doesn't matter concedes the framing; magnitude-times-probability is your honest strongest ground.

steps.prompt: What does "collapsing the round" mean?
choices: Choosing the decisive clashes and openly setting aside the rest
Giving up
Speaking as fast as possible to cover everything
Interrupting the opponent's closing
steps.explanation: Collapse is prioritisation made visible to the judge: "This round comes down to two questions..." It signals command, not surrender.

title: Structure They Can Hear
objective: Use signposting, pace and sentence length so a listener never gets lost.

steps.heading: Signpost out loud
steps.body: Listeners can't re-read. Number your points ("My first argument... my second..."), flag transitions ("Now to rebuttal"), and end each point with its impact. Spoken structure is a courtesy that judges score.

steps.heading: Sentences you can breathe through
steps.body: Long written sentences die when spoken. Aim for one idea per sentence, pause at full stops, and slow down for your most important line rather than speeding up. A deliberate pause before your key comparison is worth ten adjectives.

steps.prompt: You have 30 seconds left and two points remaining. Best move?
choices: Deliver one point properly and name-drop the other in a sentence
Rush both at double speed
Stop early to seem confident
Start a brand-new argument
steps.explanation: One completed argument scores; two half-arguments don't. Time pressure is a prioritisation test disguised as a speaking test.

steps.prompt: Which habit most helps a listening judge?
choices: Numbering arguments and stating each one's impact before moving on
Sophisticated vocabulary throughout
Speaking without any pauses to show fluency
Saving all structure for the closing
steps.explanation: Numbered points with stated impacts give the judge a flowchart of your case in real time. Vocabulary and speed impress far less than trackability.

title: Closings People Remember
objective: End with a comparison and one repeatable sentence, not a summary.

steps.heading: A closing is a verdict, not a recap
steps.body: Weak closings list everything said. Strong closings tell the judge how to decide: "If you believe X, we win; and here is why you should believe X." Frame the choice between two worlds and make yours concrete.

steps.heading: The one repeatable sentence
steps.body: Judges deliberate with whatever survives in memory. Give them one sentence that captures your decisive reason — vivid, short, and honest. "Defaults decide what millions see; we simply hand that decision back" travels further than a minute of restated points.

steps.prompt: Which is the strongest closing line for a school-phone-ban debate (For)?
choices: Six hours of attention a day is the one thing schools can still give every child — we give it back
In conclusion, we made three arguments which I will now repeat
The other side was wrong about everything
Phones are bad, thank you
steps.explanation: It's concrete, comparative and repeatable. Recaps waste the final impression; insults cost credibility; bare assertions weigh nothing.

steps.prompt: Emotional appeals in a closing are:
choices: Legitimate when tied to real stakeholders your analysis already proved are affected
Always manipulation and must be avoided
A replacement for weighing
Only for beginner audiences
steps.explanation: Emotion earned by analysis is persuasion; emotion instead of analysis is manipulation. Judges — human and AI — score the difference.

title: Questions That Corner
objective: Ask short questions that force commitments you can use later.

steps.heading: Questions are traps, not speeches
steps.body: Cross-examination isn't a chance to lecture with a question mark at the end. Ask short, closed questions that force your opponent to commit: to a number, a mechanism, or a trade-off. Then use the commitment in your next speech — an unused answer is a wasted question.

steps.heading: The commitment ladder
steps.body: Start narrow and factual ("Does your plan apply to hospitals?"), then force the trade-off ("So nurses lose shift flexibility — is that a price you accept?"). Two linked questions beat five scattered ones.

steps.prompt: Which is the best cross-examination question?
choices: What is the exact mechanism by which your ban reduces consumption?
Don't you agree your whole case is flawed?
Let me explain the seven reasons you're wrong — thoughts?
Why are you so confident?
steps.explanation: It demands a specific commitment they must defend for the rest of the round. The others invite speeches, provoke, or ask about feelings.

steps.prompt: Your opponent concedes under questioning that their policy exempts small firms. You should:
choices: Use it in your next speech to show most of the harm they claim to fix continues
Move on — the concession speaks for itself
Celebrate immediately
Ask the same question again for emphasis
steps.explanation: Concessions only score when connected to the round's decisive comparison. The judge needs you to say why the exemption guts their impact.

title: British Parliamentary in Ten Minutes
objective: Know the four teams, eight speakers, and what "extension" means.

steps.heading: Four teams, one motion
steps.body: BP has four teams of two: Opening Government, Opening Opposition, Closing Government, Closing Opposition. All four are ranked against each other — you can 'win' from any position, including by beating the team on your own side.

steps.heading: The extension
steps.body: Closing teams must add something new — an 'extension': a fresh argument, a deeper mechanism, or new weighing. Repeating your opening team's case scores nothing. The best extensions reframe what the round is really about.

steps.prompt: You're Closing Government. Opening Government already made the economic case well. You should:
choices: Extend with a distinct argument — say, the social or rights-based case — plus round-level weighing
Repeat the economic case with better delivery
Attack Opening Government to look independent
Concede to Opening Opposition
steps.explanation: The extension must be genuinely new material that closes the round. You support your bench while outshining it — never by attacking it directly.

steps.prompt: Points of Information (POIs) are:
choices: Short interjections offered during opposing speeches, which speakers should take one or two of
Written notes passed to the judge
Only allowed in the final speech
A way to run out the opponent's clock by force
steps.explanation: POIs are 15-second interventions the speaker may accept or wave down. Taking one or two and answering crisply signals command of the round.

title: Speaking Under Pressure
objective: Turn nerves into pace control and recover cleanly from losing your thread.

steps.heading: Nerves are fuel with bad steering
steps.body: Adrenaline speeds you up; audiences read speed as panic. The counter-move is mechanical, not psychological: plant your feet, breathe out fully before you begin, and deliver your first sentence slower than feels natural. Control of the first ten seconds buys the rest.

steps.heading: The recovery move
steps.body: When you lose your thread, don't apologise or restart. Bridge: repeat your last point's impact in different words while your structure reloads — "...and that is exactly why families come out ahead. Which brings me to my second argument." Judges barely notice a confident bridge.

steps.prompt: You blank completely mid-speech. Best recovery?
choices: Restate your previous impact, then move to your next numbered point
Apologise and start the speech again
Stand silent until it returns
Admit you forgot and ask the judge for help
steps.explanation: The bridge keeps authority intact and gives your memory a familiar landmark — your own structure — to reboot from.

steps.prompt: The most effective slow-down technique is:
choices: Pausing deliberately at full stops, especially before key lines
Adding filler words to stretch time
Reading directly from notes
Speaking quietly
steps.explanation: Pauses create emphasis and thinking room without diluting content. Fillers and reading kill the connection pauses create.

title: Persuasion Beyond the Podium
objective: Apply debate structure to meetings, pitches and negotiations.

steps.heading: Meetings are unjudged debates
steps.body: A pitch is an opening speech; an objection is rebuttal; a negotiation is weighing. The same chain applies: claim, mechanism, example, impact — except your 'judge' is a decision-maker with ten other things on their mind, so lead with the impact.

steps.heading: Answer the strongest objection first
steps.body: In professional settings, unaddressed objections don't get speeches — they get silent vetoes. Name the strongest objection to your own proposal before anyone else does, answer it, and you remove its power while earning trust.

steps.prompt: Opening a budget request to a distracted executive, lead with:
choices: The impact: what the money returns and by when
The full history of the project
Your methodology
An apology for taking their time
steps.explanation: Executives triage by impact. History and methodology are supporting material for after you've earned attention — apology spends credibility for nothing.

steps.prompt: Pre-empting your proposal's weakest point ("steelmanning the objection") works because:
choices: It removes the objection's surprise value and signals you've thought it through
It fills time
It confuses opponents
It lowers expectations
steps.explanation: Objections are most powerful when they appear to have been hidden. Raising and answering them yourself converts a vulnerability into evidence of rigour.

title: Framing: Deciding What the Round Is About
objective: Set the decision rule early so every later argument lands on your terms.

steps.heading: Whoever frames, wins
steps.body: Before arguments clash, frames clash: is this round about freedom or safety? Cost or fairness? The side that establishes the decision rule — "this debate is decided by which side protects the most vulnerable" — makes every subsequent argument play on home turf.

steps.heading: Contesting a frame
steps.body: Never silently accept the opponent's frame. Either broaden it ("safety matters, but so does who pays for it"), replace it with justification ("the real question is X, because..."), or capture it ("under their own frame, we still win"). Capturing is the most devastating — and hardest.

steps.prompt: Opponent frames a surveillance debate as "safety versus privacy — and safety wins." The strongest response?
choices: Capture it: show mass surveillance fails to deliver the safety they promise
Ignore the frame and list your own points
Accept the frame and argue privacy anyway
Complain that framing is unfair
steps.explanation: Winning inside their own frame leaves them nowhere to retreat. Ignoring frames means the judge decides by their rule — with your arguments orphaned outside it.

steps.prompt: A decision rule should be introduced:
choices: In your opening, with a justification for why it's the fair test
Only in the closing, as a surprise
Never explicitly
Only if the opponent introduces one first
steps.explanation: Early framing shapes how the judge files every later argument. A closing-speech frame arrives after the filing cabinet is full.
